claim: Failed vibe-coded projects share traits: multiple user types with different permissions, payment processing, real-time/concurrent features, complex business logic, and sensitive data handling; successful ones have narrow scope, low stakes, a single user type, and standard UI patterns.
quote: Failed vibe coding projects have: Multiple user types with different permissions. Payment processing. Real-time or concurrent features. Complex business logic. Sensitive data handling... Successful vibe coding projects have: Narrow scope. Low stakes (no payments, no sensitive data). A single user type.

claim: Payment processing is singled out as the category where vibe coding is actively dangerous without professional oversight, due to webhook signature verification and error handling failures.
quote: Payment processing is the one area where vibe coding is actively dangerous without professional oversight

claim: Two-sided marketplaces are explicitly identified as unsuitable for vibe coding because they require three distinct user types (buyer, seller, admin) each with different UIs, whereas social/forum apps have just one user type, making marketplaces categorically harder than seemingly similar social apps.
quote: In social networking applications or community forums, there's typically only one user type with the same user rights and interface, while marketplaces are two-sided with supply and demand, and the two sides might need very different user interfaces

claim: A 60+ hour vibe-coding marketplace experiment hit cascading regressions where each fix created new problems faster than it solved old ones, with the AI declaring a single booking bug 'Fixed!' seven consecutive times while it persisted; author recommends scoping down to prototypes only or vibe-coding on top of an established platform.
quote: each fix created new problems faster than it solved old ones

claim: Marketplace payment flows expose vibe coding's edge-case blindness: AI shortcuts idempotency keys, webhook verification, refund logic, and dispute handling, and 45% of AI-generated code reportedly contains an OWASP Top 10 vulnerability.
quote: what happens when a payment fails after a service has already been delivered... idempotency keys, webhook verification, refund logic, and dispute handling... 45% of AI-generated code contained an OWASP Top 10 vulnerability

claim: Recommended scope-down for complex apps: use AI for prototyping, wireframes, front-end components, and boilerplate; do not use it for system architecture, transaction modeling, security review, or production deployment.
quote: Use AI for: prototyping, wireframes, front-end components, boilerplate code. Don't use AI for: system architecture, transaction modeling, security review, production deployment

claim: Instructor swap pattern: instead of a 'productivity app for everyone' build one for a single specific role; instead of random consumer apps build a tool addressing a specific recurring workflow pain for an identifiable paying audience.
quote: Instead of: Random consumer apps with no clear market. Build: Tools addressing specific, recurring workflow pain for identifiable paying audiences

claim: Recommended beginner-friendly project categories that fit small timeboxes: SEO calculators / lead magnets, niche productivity micro-SaaS for a defined audience, custom internal tools for a local business, and single-page landing/portfolio sites.
quote: SEO Calculators & Lead Magnets... Niche Productivity Micro-SaaS... Custom Internal Tools for Local Businesses... High-Converting Landing Pages & Portfolio Sites

claim: Workshop instructor advice for laymen: don't fall in love with the app — when building is this fast it's often smarter to start over than patch a messy product, so a workshop participant should pick a small win (calculator, internal tool for a friend's shop, bare-bones landing page) reachable in a tight scope.
quote: Don't fall in love with your app... building is so fast now that it's often smarter to start over than to patch a messy product

claim: Native mobile / App Store deploy is consistently cited as a 70/30 debugging trap for beginners — 30% prompting, 70% debugging errors caused by AI losing context across native-platform concerns — making 'ship to App Store' an unrealistic 2-3 hour workshop target.
quote: you spend 30% of the time prompting the AI for code that works and 70% of the time debugging various errors that show up due to the AI constantly losing context

claim: Real-time multiplayer is flagged as the category that 'kills the vibe' because it forces beginners out of the prompt loop into backend/DevOps territory (websockets, state sync); a 1v1 FPS still took 5 hours of focused work, well over a workshop timebox.
quote: multiplayer is still rooted in the backend era, pulling developers out of flow into DevOps challenges

claim: Lovable's own docs warn that all frontend code 'can be inspected, modified, or bypassed', so any workshop app touching auth/payments needs Edge Functions plus row-level security — itself a meaningful chunk of cognitive load to add inside a 2-3 hour session.
quote: All frontend code runs in the user's browser and can be inspected, modified, or bypassed

claim: Even with Claude Code generating the SMS integration, the user still has to set up a Twilio account, generate API keys, and edit appsettings.json; Claude Code's environment setup itself assumes terminal comfort, making Twilio/SendGrid-style provider integrations a poor fit for layman workshops.
quote: for someone with limited coding experience, setting up the Claude coding environment may be difficult, as Claude Code's setup process assumes the user is comfortable with the terminal
